Adult males of Bonga (Ethmalosa fimbriata) from the Senegalese coast reach a maximum total length of 45 centimeters [Li = 45 centimeters], a size that is among the largest recorded for clupeids inhabiting the eastern Atlantic. This ultimate length is attained after several years of continuous somatic growth, a pattern common among iteroparous clupeiform teleosts. Field surveys in the Sine-Saloum estuary indicate that puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence, occurs at a total length of 17 centimeters [Lp = 17 centimeters], a size threshold that corresponds to the initial allocation of resources toward reproductive tissues rather than further somatic expansion. Individuals at this length typically weigh approximately 54 grams [Wwp = approximately 54 grams], a body mass that reflects the energetic condition necessary for successful vitellogenesis and spermiation. The length at puberty is notably smaller than the asymptotic length, a pattern consistent with early maturation in response to high natural mortality rates in estuarine environments. Comparative data from other West African clupeids suggest that this length-based maturation schedule is shaped by local temperature regimes and food availability.

The wet weight at birth of Ethmalosa fimbriata is remarkably low at only 0.0141 grams [Wwb = 0.0141 grams], derived from an oocyte diameter of 3 millimeters typical of the closely related Alosa alosa. This minimal initial mass reflects the energetic constraints of producing large numbers of small pelagic eggs, a strategy common among small-bodied clupeiform teleosts. The eggs are transparent and slightly buoyant, undergoing external fertilisation during broadcast spawning events in the brackish waters of estuaries and coastal lagoons. The yolk-sac larva that emerges upon eclosion is entirely dependent on endogenous reserves, with the chorion rupture occurring approximately 48 hours after fertilisation at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. During this lecithotrophic phase, the prolarva measures roughly 3.5 millimeters in standard length and remains non-feeding until mouth opening and retinal differentiation enable first prey capture. The transition to exogenous nutrition is a critical bottleneck; larvae failing to encounter suitable zooplankton within the point of no return window suffer irreversible physiological deterioration. These findings highlight the vulnerability of the yolk-sac stage to fluctuations in estuarine productivity.

Under the stable thermal regime of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], mature females of Ethmalosa fimbriata exhibit a batch spawning strategy characterized by a high individual egg output. Each spawning event yields approximately 50,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 50,000 eggs per clutch], and females typically engage in approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year] during the warm, productive upwelling period from May to October. This high reproductive output is energetically demanding and reflects the selective pressure of high larval mortality in turbid estuarine habitats.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Ethmalosa fimbriata is approximately 1,050 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,050 grams], a mass that is achieved only by the largest, oldest individuals in the population, typically females in prime reproductive condition. This asymptotic body mass is derived from a length-weight relationship that describes a slightly positively allometric growth pattern characteristic of many clupeids that accumulate visceral fat deposits during the productive season. Individuals reaching this upper mass are rare in heavily exploited stocks, where fishing mortality truncates the size distribution well before the physiological maximum can be realized. Histological examination of gonads from individuals exceeding 1,000 grams reveals extensive vitellogenic oocytes, indicating that these large females contribute disproportionately to the annual egg production of the population. The 54 gram [Wwp = 54 gram] threshold marking puberty represents less than six percent of the maximum adult mass, a pattern underscoring the extensive post-maturation growth characteristic of indeterminate growers that continue adding somatic tissue long after the onset of reproductive activity.

The maximum lifespan of Ethmalosa fimbriata is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] under stable thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], an intermediate value among West African clupeids that exceeds the 4-year lifespan of Sardinella aurita but falls short of the 12-year maximum recorded for the larger Ilisha africana. Senescence in this species is characterized by a progressive decline in fecundity and egg quality, with the oldest individuals producing smaller clutches of less viable oocytes. The age at first reproduction, which for most females occurs at around 18 months after hatching [tR = 18 months after hatching], represents a relatively early maturation schedule that compensates for high juvenile mortality. In exploited populations, the selective removal of large, old individuals has shifted the demographic structure toward younger age classes, reducing the average reproductive contribution of the spawning stock. This truncation of the age structure may ultimately affect the population's resilience to environmental variability, as the loss of old, iteroparous females reduces the portfolio effect that buffers against poor recruitment years.
